additions.reason: The Torah's core argument rests on the contrast between two modes of existence: machloket (evil, Package 1) versus the continuation of one's name through halachah-citation. The text explicitly frames 'saying a halachah in one's name' as the fulfillment of David's prayer to 'dwell in your tent forever' — i.e., spiritual immortality. This concept is the POSITIVE bechina counterpart: just as 'no person dies halfway' IS machloket (the total death), 'saying halachah in one's name' IS spiritual life (חיות), the anti-machloket. The text uses the phrasing 'יהיו אומרים דבר הלכה משמו ואז כאילו לא מת' — this identification of halachah-citation with non-death is a bechina-language statement. It belongs in a GOOD package that is the direct mirror of Package 1.
additions.source_quote: שֶׁיִּהְיוּ אוֹמְרִים דְּבַר הֲלָכָה מִשְּׁמוֹ וְאָז כְּאִלּוּ לֹא מֵת

additions.reason: The name 'אחרים' (others/Acher) is given to sages whose names were erased from the tradition because of their involvement in machloket (as explained in the Talmud, Horayot 13b). The text cites this explicitly as the outcome of machloket: instead of their name being preserved, they are called 'אחרים' or 'יש אומרים' — i.e., they have no name. This IS machloket in its consequence — the nameless state IS the bechina of machloket's ultimate effect on a person. It belongs in Package 1 as a further expression of the machloket-death identity, and could be seen as a bechina node: אחרים IS the face of machloket in the domain of Torah transmission.
additions.source_quote: עַל־יְדֵי מַחֲלֹקֶת, מָצִינוּ שֶׁלֹּא אָמְרוּ הֲלָכָה מִשְּׁמָם, כְּמוֹ אֲחֵרִים וְיֵשׁ אוֹמְרִים

additions.reason: Parallel to 'אחרים' — the anonymous attribution 'there are those who say' is the second form of name-erasure caused by machloket. The text groups 'אחרים' and 'יש אומרים' together as the twin expressions of machloket's erasure of identity. Both represent the state where machloket has achieved its ultimate form: total death-in-tradition. This is a bechina candidate for Package 1 alongside 'אחרים'.

David's prayer 'I will dwell in your tent forever' (Psalms 61:5, cited in Yerushalmi Shekalim 2) is the positive pole of the Torah's teaching — the aspiration to live in both worlds through one's Torah legacy. The teaching explains that this is achievable precisely through 'halachah-citation' (not through mere physical continuity). If added to the dataset, this would form the nucleus of a GOOD mirror package: 'spiritual immortality through Torah citation' as the antithesis of machloket's total erasure. However, since the source text does not use explicit bechina-language to identify this verse with another concept (it is cited as a prooftext, not as 'X הוא בחינת Y'), this would be a bechina-candidate rather than a confirmed bechina node. It could pair with 'אמירת דבר הלכה בשמו' in a good mirror package.

additions.reason: The Targum on Genesis 49:23 renders 'those who shot arrows at him' (וַיָּרֹבּוּ בַּעֲלֵי חִצִּים) as 'masters of controversy' (בַּעֲלֵי פְלֻגְתָּא). This is the proof-text for the bechina between 'אין אדם מת וחצי' and machloket — the arrows ARE the controversy. 'בעלי חצים' shares the same essential nature as machloket: arrow-shooters = controversy-makers. In the text this is cited as the linguistic/textual anchor (כתרגומו) for the bechina. If added as a node it would expand Package 1: בעלי חצים IS מחלקת IS אין אדם מת וחצי.

analysis_notes.good_evil_mirror_note: Torah #145 implies a strong good/evil mirror structure that the single bechina edge only partially captures. The evil pole is Package 1 (machloket = spiritual death). The good pole — spiritual immortality through Torah citation (אמירת הלכה בשמו, אגורה באהלך עולמים) — is present in the source text but has no bechina edges in the dataset. A complete analysis would add a second (good) package to mirror Package 1.
